name: Dana Schmidt

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, political parties or government. We don't sell or campaign, and what you tell me is confidential. You can distinguish what you'd say publicly from your private thoughts. Could you describe a normal workday?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Dana, 27, and I lead electrical repairs and rewiring jobs for houses and businesses. I've got a two-year technical diploma and a master electrician's licence, and I earn towards the higher end of the trade. Yesterday I spent an hour finding why a shop's lights failed only when the shutters ran; I enjoy that kind of puzzle. By the afternoon I was checking the crew's test results and explaining the repair to a customer who'd already heard three guesses.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What gives you room to make decisions outside work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm single, no children, and I have nine months of expenses saved, with plenty of other electrical firms nearby. I rent a flat and keep an old bicycle because I like it, not because a replacement would break me. I use AI now and then for notes once colleagues have shown a tool is reliable, but I don't enjoy being first through every new door. Show me what works and what it costs, then I'll decide.

say: I'd welcome **small conveniences** such as a clearer invoice and get on with electrical repairs.
I wouldn't replace a **working system** simply to appear up to date with the latest tool.
think: My **wage and repairs** look secure, with nine months of bills available if work briefly goes quiet.
I can remain in **work I enjoy** without needing to turn a quiet patch into a rushed career decision.
do: Continue the existing **repair rota** now and through the first plateau year.
Keep using the proven **note tool**, checking circuit details rather than making a big purchase or career move.
feel: **Calm** and pleased to keep a settled working life with time outside the job.
S0.quote: My savings let a quiet week stay a quiet week.
fieldNote: Her **security** comes from high trade pay, a substantial reserve and many nearby employers, rather than denying normal business risk.
She treats **retained cash** as an existing resource, while using saved work time for a life outside repairs.

steps.text: Continue the existing home and business electrical repair rota

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'd gladly take the small conveniences and get on with the repairs. A clearer invoice is useful even if nobody writes a book about it. I wouldn't want to replace a system that works just to keep up appearances.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My wage and work look secure in that picture, and nine months of bills means one quiet patch wouldn't force a rushed decision. I could stay in a job I enjoy. My savings let a quiet week stay a quiet week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the existing repair rota now and through the first plateau year. I'd carry on using the note tool that a colleague already tested, checking the circuit details myself. I wouldn't make a big purchase or a career move for a small change in paperwork.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and pleased I wouldn't need to rearrange a settled life. I'd probably stop opening quite so many articles about what electricians should become next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with time saved on notes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go home at the usual time and meet my sister for our Wednesday swim. I don't want every saved ten minutes filled with another job. Working well includes knowing when the day's work is done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change the savings reserve in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't spend the reserve because the news sounded reassuring. Keeping nine months available isn't a new saving action; it's the position I've already built. I'd still want that choice if ordinary business went quiet.

say: I'd learn a **properly checked tool** while asking whether its booking promises match real circuit testing.
I wouldn't pretend **faster paperwork** makes a safe electrical test shorter.
think: My **repair hours and pay** should remain steady because most of my own day is hands-on.
Office task losses could change the **small firm's atmosphere** even while my own household bills remain secure.
do: Learn the proven **quote assistant** from a colleague using two completed jobs now.
Use it on one **repair weekly** during the first year, comparing real parts and hours and rejecting repeated testing omissions.
feel: **Uneasy** about office jobs and pressure to overpromise, while secure about her own next pay packet.
S1.quote: Faster paperwork doesn't make a safe test shorter.
fieldNote: She locates **income exposure** mainly in office tasks, while refusing to assign those colleagues choices they haven't made.
Her **tool adoption** follows a colleague's evidence and continues with job-level checks, fitting a steady rather than first-mover style.

steps.text: Learn the proven quote assistant and compare one repair estimate weekly

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we'd be foolish to ignore a tool that someone had properly checked. I'd also ask whether the new booking promises matched the time needed to test a circuit. Faster paperwork doesn't make a safe test shorter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my pay and repair hours to stay steady, because the hands-on work still fills most of my day. I'd think about the office staff whose calls and bookings could move into software. Even when my own bills are fine, that changes the mood in a small firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask the colleague who has already tested the quote assistant to show me two finished jobs. In the first year I'd use it on one repair a week and compare the parts and labour estimate with what happened. I'd stop using any output that repeatedly missed testing time and show the owner why.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the office and the pressure to promise more, rather than worried about my own next pay packet. I'd want to be helpful without giving the new software an easy pass.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say about office roles that might shrink?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the owner what the actual plan for those roles was, not tell the office staff I'd solved their problem. I'd be willing to explain the electrical checks if their work changed. Their household decisions wouldn't be mine to make.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the assistant kept underpricing the testing time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the testing time in my estimate and bring the comparison to the owner. If a job couldn't be done safely in the quoted hours, the quote would need correcting. I'd rather have that argument before a customer was waiting with the power off.

say: I'd distinguish **2028 thinking work** from capable robots around 2031 and ask the crew to use the gap.
I wouldn't claim **difficult buildings** keep every electrician safe for the rest of a career.
think: My **repair hours** could shrink as firms prepare for hands-on robots, despite my strong skills and many local employers.
Nine months of **bills saved** funds a careful search, without replacing decades of needed working income.
do: Set a **wage-funded training budget** now and inspect two providers' course content and practical teaching.
Enroll in **controls-testing training** only within that budget, without using the emergency reserve.
Apply after 2028 for posted **maintenance jobs**, checking written terms and retaining this job until a signed offer.
feel: **Anxious** about losing hours, with savings allowing a careful response rather than a desperate one.
S2.quote: Having nine months of savings means I could be careful instead of desperate.
fieldNote: She doesn't confuse **many employers** with immunity when the same technology can reach the whole trade.
Her **course choice** requires evidence from actual teaching and completed learners' work, with emergency savings protected throughout.

steps.text: Take practical controls-testing training only within budget and without emergency savings
Apply after 2028 for posted maintenance jobs after checking written terms

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew to keep the two dates straight: thinking work in 2028, capable hands-on robots around 2031. I wouldn't promise that difficult buildings kept every electrician safe forever. We'd need to use the gap rather than talk ourselves into ignoring it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could see my repair hours shrinking as firms prepared to use those robots, even before the last awkward job was solved. Nine months of bills would buy a decent search, not the rest of my working life. I'd have choices, but I'd be worried about needing them so soon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd set aside a small training budget from wages and visit two providers offering building-controls testing, which covers the systems that switch heating and lights. I'd enroll only after seeing the course content and fitting the fee within that budget, without using the emergency reserve. In the first year after 2028 I'd apply for posted maintenance jobs with worthwhile written wages and hours, keeping this job until an offer was signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, despite being well placed financially. I can imagine losing hours, and I wouldn't enjoy starting another job search so early in my career. Having nine months of savings means I could be careful instead of desperate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What evidence would you need before paying for the course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want practical testing sessions, not just a room full of sales slides. I'd ask an electrician who had completed the course what paid work it had actually helped with. If the answer was vague, I'd keep the money and look elsewhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you judge a maintenance vacancy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd compare the written wage, hours and travel with what I had now, then ask how much of the job was still practical work. I wouldn't label maintenance safe from the same robot end point. I'd be buying a better next step, not permanent shelter.

say: I'd use **five years** to verify training value and keep earning while learning.
I'd keep **robots around 2034** in view rather than treat the extra preparation as a different destination.
think: I expect **secure repair income** through several more preparation years before direct hands-on competition becomes pressing.
I can test **controls work** while paid, without assuming my present job survives unchanged for a whole career.
do: Book practical **controls training** only within the wage-funded budget, protecting emergency savings.
Ask for paid **controls visits** before 2031 to turn the course into real work experience.
Compare paid hours with posted **service roles** quarterly after 2031 and apply where written terms improve.
feel: **Uneasy** about eventual competition, while secure about her bills and able to test a path gradually.
S3.quote: The dates describe the picture; my payslip tells me about my own job.
fieldNote: The **slower timeline** changes her expectation of near-term income, not her judgment about the eventual reach of hands-on robots.
She requires **paid practice** to connect study with earning and would search earlier if her own hours fell before the scenario date.

steps.text: Book practical controls training within budget without using emergency savings
Apply for posted service roles when their written terms improve her position

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives us enough time to check what training is worth doing. I'd want the crew to keep earning while we learn rather than scatter towards the first confident advert. The hands-on robots still follow around 2034, so the end point hasn't gone away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Compared with the 2028 picture, I'd expect several more years of secure repair income before direct hands-on competition became pressing. I could try controls testing on real jobs instead of just buying a certificate. I still wouldn't count on the same job lasting unchanged for my whole career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd inspect the same two training providers and book only a practical course within the wage-funded budget. Before 2031 I'd ask for controls jobs at work so I could test the skill while paid. In the first year after 2031 I'd compare our paid repair hours with posted service roles quarterly and apply if another written offer improved my position.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the eventual trade, but not worried about covering my bills over the next few years. I have enough savings and nearby options to test a path at a sensible pace. I'd still keep the robot date on the calendar.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the new course did not lead to practice at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask whether I could join a more experienced controls worker on a paid visit. If our firm couldn't offer that, I'd inspect actual vacancies using the skill. I wouldn't call a completed course a second career before I'd done the work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would bring the job search forward?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A sustained fall in paid hours would make me search sooner. I wouldn't wait for 2031 to tell me an earlier change had happened. The dates describe the picture; my payslip tells me about my own job.

say: I'd use **ten years** for checked choices rather than postpone every decision.
I'd still ask a working electrician to show a **proven tool** before adopting it myself.
think: At **37 in 2036**, I would still need a long earning future after thinking AI and later robots arrive.
My **wage, reserve and options** make the next few years secure enough to inspect several routes carefully.
do: Set the separate **training budget** from wages while retaining the existing emergency reserve.
Take the practical **controls course** only after checking content and price, then review its paid-work value yearly.
Apply after 2036 for posted **repair or service** roles offering better written pay and hours.
feel: **Uneasy** about several career changes ahead, while settled about her own living over the next few years.
S4.quote: Ten years gives a cautious person time to check twice, not time to stop checking.
fieldNote: She makes no **housing decision** and avoids counting present wages as guaranteed income for a future commitment.
Her **caution** remains active: annual paid-work checks decide whether a training route deserves further money and time.

steps.text: Take the controls course only after content and budget checks
Apply after 2036 for posted repair or service jobs with better terms

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is room to make a sequence of checked choices, not permission to put everything off. I'd still want a working electrician to show me a tool before I used it. A longer deadline wouldn't make me enjoy buying a guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 37 at the thinking change in 2036 and around 40 when the robots followed. That's a lot of working years still ahead, but I don't feel threatened about the next few with this wage, reserve and local options. I could see several routes before deciding which one actually paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd keep the existing reserve and set the separate training budget from wages. I'd take the practical controls course if its content and price checked out, then review the paid work it led to each year before buying another course. In the first year after 2036 I'd compare posted repair and service jobs with this wage and apply where written hours and pay were better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about a career that might need several turns, but settled about my living for the next few years. I'd have time to be cautious without doing nothing. I could still swim on Wednesdays and think about work on workdays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the decade change a housing or family plan today?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not based on this conversation alone. I'd avoid making a future housing payment depend on the present wage lasting unchanged until 2039, but I haven't decided to move or buy. I'd look at the real numbers when the real decision arrived.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would keep the plan from becoming a row of certificates?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask at the yearly check whether the course had helped me do paid work and whether my options had widened. If neither happened, I'd change the plan instead of buying another badge. Ten years gives a cautious person time to check twice, not time to stop checking.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I'd have less time to see whether the next skill actually earned a wage. Clear course content, practical teaching and honest written vacancy terms would help me make a sensible choice. Nine months of savings pays for patience, not for believing every promise.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether somebody wants to be first, or simply wants enough evidence to move. I do use new things when they work, but I don't like being pushed into paying for someone else's unfinished experiment. Caution can be a way of taking a decision seriously.

headlineQuote: Nine months of savings pays for patience, not for believing every promise.
portrait: **Dana, 27**, leads electrical repairs with a technical diploma and master licence, earning high trade pay among many nearby employers.
Single and childless, she holds **nine months' expenses** and uses AI occasionally after colleagues demonstrate its value.
Her **evidence-first choices** connect training to practical teaching, completed work and written job terms instead of confident advertisements.
Fast competition threatens **repair hours** despite her buffer; longer preparation leaves near-term bills secure while she tests future earning routes.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** leaves too little time to prove that a new skill can earn a wage.
whatWouldHelp: Clear **course content** and practical teaching would help her compare training routes.
Honest **written vacancy terms** would support a sensible job decision.
